title: Identity, authentication, MFA and least privilege
subtitle: Design safer access, strong authentication, account recovery and regular privilege review.
description: Design safer access, strong authentication, account recovery and regular privilege review. Guided explanations, six original visual diagrams, safe practice, trusted resource links, worked examples and a randomized quiz.

blocks.text: Lesson 3 — Identity, authentication, MFA and least privilege

LEARNING OUTCOME
Design safer access, strong authentication, account recovery and regular privilege review.

Safety rule: work only with devices, accounts and training applications you own or have explicit written permission to assess. Use synthetic information. A public system or a suspicious person is not permission.

Authentication answers “who is this identity?” Authorization answers “what may it do?” A successful sign-in must not automatically grant access to every record. Enforce authorization on the server for each protected action, even if a user modifies a URL or submits an API request directly.

blocks.text: Use unique accounts, MFA or passkeys where supported, secure recovery, appropriate session expiry and alerts for risky changes. Store passwords with a vetted password-specific hashing scheme and unique salts; never save raw passwords or log secrets. Unexpected MFA prompts should be denied and reported.

blocks.caption: Visual 3/6 — Least privilege. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.
Visual 4/6 — Role mapping. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Joiner-mover-leaver processes create, change, review and remove access. Service identities need owners and narrow permissions; rotate or revoke exposed credentials. Periodic access reviews should be evidence-based and record who approved exceptions.

Visual 6/6 — Access review. Use it to explain how the controls or workflow connect.

blocks.text: Practice checklist: (1) read the lab rules, (2) use fabricated data or an isolated training target, (3) predict what the control should do, (4) test one small condition, (5) save only minimal evidence, and (6) explain the defensive follow-up. Stop and ask the owner if any target or action is outside the approved scope.

blocks.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks allowed actions
blocks.explanation: A valid sign-in never grants all possible access by itself.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Which action best protects a sensitive server account?
options: Use MFA and grant only role-required permissions
Share one password across the team
blocks.explanation: MFA and least privilege reduce account compromise impact.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: Which approach better protects private information?
options: Use synthetic data and collect only necessary, authorized evidence
Copy all customer records for convenience
blocks.explanation: Data minimization and redaction reduce privacy and exposure risks.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What is a sound step after applying a fix?
options: Retest the same authorized condition and document the result
blocks.explanation: Retesting verifies the correction and preserves a useful record.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.

blocks.question: What should happen when a target is outside scope?
options: Stop and ask the owner to clarify permission
blocks.explanation: Scope is a boundary; do not proceed without permission.
blocks.hint: Use the lesson definitions and authorization boundary to reason through the options.
